hints: Follow reaction 2 first. Excess concentrated ammonia replaces both water and hydroxide ligands around cobalt(II) to give a soluble hexaammine complex.
Follow reaction 3. Carbonate ions precipitate cobalt(II) directly from the hexaaqua ion as a neutral carbonate salt.
walkthrough:
Track what excess ammonia does**
You start from $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{OH})_2]$. With a little ammonia you get this neutral hydroxide precipitate, but with a large excess the $\text{NH}_3$ molecules are strong enough ligands to push out all the $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ groups. Cobalt(II) keeps coordination number 6, so you end with six ammonias bound: $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$, which is soluble, so it is a solution of A.

Track what carbonate does**
$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ removes $\text{Co}^{2+}$ from solution as an insoluble salt. No change in oxidation state occurs, Co stays as +2. The neutral precipitate is simply cobalt(II) carbonate, $\text{CoCO}_3$.

Final answer: A = $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$
B = $\text{CoCO}_3$

hints: Reaction 1 converts $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ to $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{OH})_2]$ by replacing two waters with hydroxides, so think which common base supplies $\text{OH}^-$.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydroxide formation**
Reaction 1 is the classic test for a +2 metal: hexaaqua to dihydroxo-tetraaqua precipitate. That needs hydroxide ions, so you add dilute sodium hydroxide solution, $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.
Final answer: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ or $\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$

hints: Write the neutral hydroxide complex plus $\text{NH}_3$ on the left and the hexaammine product plus displaced $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}^-$ on the right, then balance ligands and charge.
walkthrough:
Balance the ligand swap**
Six $\text{NH}_3$ molecules come in. Four $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules are pushed out as water and two $\text{OH}^-$ groups are pushed out as hydroxide ions. Check atoms and charge: left neutral + neutral, right $2+$ plus $2-$ gives neutral overall. That gives $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{OH})_2] + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2\text{OH}^-$.

hints: Combine $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ with $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ to give solid $\text{CoCO}_3$ and free water, then balance the six waters.
walkthrough:
Write the precipitation cleanly**
The six water ligands are simply released when the ionic lattice forms. Charges cancel $2+$ with $2-$ to give neutral products: $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{CoCO}_3 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Recall the key property that lets transition metals shuttle electrons in redox catalysis by cycling between two stable charged states.
walkthrough:
Link catalysis to electron transfer**
A redox catalyst must be oxidised and then reduced back. Cobalt can exist stably as $\text{Co}^{2+}$ and $\text{Co}^{3+}$, so it can accept and donate electrons in turn and be regenerated. That variable oxidation state behaviour is the reason it works.
Final answer: Ability to show variable oxidation states

hints: The parent acid is $\text{HOOC-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-COOH}$, and the ion $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$ has lost both carboxylic protons, so draw two $\text{COO}^-$ ends with central CH(OH) groups.
walkthrough:
Build the dianion**
Start with 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid: a four carbon chain, carboxylic acid groups at C1 and C4, and an OH on each of C2 and C3. Remove $\text{H}^+$ from both $\text{COOH}$ groups to give $\text{COO}^-$ at each end. You are left with $^-\text{OOC-C(H)(OH)-C(H)(OH)-COO}^-$, which is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$.
Final answer: $^-\text{OOC-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-COO}^-$, with two central C atoms each bonded to one H and one OH, and each end as $\text{COO}^-$

hints: Use [O] as requested. Balance carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and the overall charge.
walkthrough: Two carbon atoms form two HCO₂⁻ ions; the other two form two CO₂ molecules. Adding H₂O balances hydrogen. Three [O] atoms are then required to balance oxygen; the total charge is −2 on each side.
Final answer: $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}+3[\text{O}]\rightarrow 2\text{HCO}_2^-+2\text{CO}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: $\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$ is square planar with Pt at the centre, so sketch a square with four positions for the two $\text{NH}_3$ and two $\text{Cl}$ ligands.
Place identical ligands next to each other at 90 degrees for cis and opposite each other at 180 degrees for trans.
walkthrough:
Fix the shape first**
$\text{Pt(II)}$ with coordination number 4 is square planar, not tetrahedral. Draw Pt in the middle of a square with four bonds to the corners. That flat shape is what allows cis and trans forms to exist and be distinct.

Place ligands to show the isomers**
For cis-$\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$, put the two $\text{NH}_3$ groups on neighbouring corners so they are 90 degrees apart, with the two Cl also neighbouring. For trans, put the two $\text{NH}_3$ groups across from each other at 180 degrees, with the two Cl also across from each other. Label each box clearly.

Final answer: Square planar drawings: cis isomer has the two $\text{NH}_3$ adjacent (90 degrees) and the two Cl adjacent; trans isomer has the two $\text{NH}_3$ opposite (180 degrees) and the two Cl opposite, both correctly labelled.

hints: Think about what cis-platin binds to inside the cell nucleus after losing its chloride ligands.
Consider what happens to cell growth if DNA cannot be copied correctly.
walkthrough:
Bind to the target**
Once inside the cell, cis-platin exchanges its chloride ligands and bonds directly to DNA bases. It forms crosslinks within the DNA strand.

Block growth**
That damage distorts the double helix so enzymes cannot copy it. Without DNA replication, mitosis and cell division stop, which is why it kills rapidly dividing cancer cells.

Final answer: Cis-platin can react with / bind to DNA.
This prevents replication of the strand / prevents cell division / prevents mitosis.

hints: The two $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands leave and the cyclobutane-1,1-dicarboxylate ion uses one oxygen from each $\text{COO}^-$ group to bond to Pt, forming a chelate ring while the two $\text{NH}_3$ groups stay in cis positions.
walkthrough:
Swap monodentate for bidentate**
Keep the cis-$\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2$ unit exactly as it is. Remove the two $\text{Cl}^-$. The $[\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_4]^{2-}$ ion has two $\text{COO}^-$ arms on the same cyclobutane carbon. Each arm donates one oxygen lone pair to Pt, so Pt is bonded to two O atoms, making a six membered chelate ring. That bidentate complex plus $2\text{Cl}^-$ on the right is carboplatin.

Final answer: Carboplatin is $\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2$ bonded through two Pt-O bonds to the two carboxylate groups of $[\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_4]^{2-}$, forming a bidentate chelate with cis $\text{NH}_3$ groups retained.
